doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Bands as displays of ability rather than units
summary: He laments that today's musicians each show off instead of playing as a team.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: But that was his philosophy. Okay? If this guy match with me, if he plays what I’m hearing, he’s going to be in. If he doesn’t play what I’m hearing that means that we both we don’t match and I’m going to continue looking for the perfect match. But all the musicians, they demand, “If I’m singing please use this cymbal because it will not be the same one because the frequency, my voice range, I want you to play soft here” and so forth and so on. It was a music lesson. You were at a conservatory or at a jazz university and you learn. And culturally nowadays I see musicians getting on the bandstand and everybody plays. It is a display of musical abilities. “Oh I’m going to show you how can I do this and that.” In most cases I don’t see any, it’s hard to see a band that plays as a unit, as a team. Everybody is a star. Everybody plays for themselves. That’s my appreciation. I don’t want people to think that what I’m saying is the rule. From my © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
perspective, what I have been seeing it is what has been happening from a while back. For a while.
